title: Near-Optimal and Efficient First-Order Algorithm for Multi-Task Learning with Shared Linear Representation
claim: Ours reaches the theoretical error bound after a phase switch, while all baselines converge slowly and stay above it.
layout: 3 line-plot panels in a row, shared legend, dashed phase-switch line
description: Three side-by-side log-scale line plots show estimation error (y-axis) against training iteration (x-axis). Each panel uses a different problem size (d=100,k=10,T=100,N=1000; d=200,k=20,T=200,N=1000; d=400,k=50,T=400,N=2000). Each panel plots a blue TPGD curve, red and green GD with Loss 1 and Loss 2, and an orange NSGD curve. A dashed purple horizontal line marks the theoretical error bound. A grey dashed vertical line marks the Phase I/II switch. All curves start at a high plateau and decay slowly. After the switch the blue TPGD curve drops sharply below the theoretical bound and flattens. The baselines stay above the bound, and in the larger panels they have barely moved by the end. The legend sits inside each panel, and the eye goes first to the blue cliff.
caption: The convergence rates between TPGD and the comparative algorithms with fixed per-task sample size N. The vertical axis represents the last-iterate estimation error, while the horizontal axis denotes the number of training iterations.
abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) has emerged as a pivotal paradigm in machine learning by leveraging shared structures across multiple related tasks. Despite its empirical success, the development of likelihood-based efficiently solvable algorithms--even for shared linear representations--remains largely underdeveloped, primarily due to the non-convex structure intrinsic to matrix factorization. This paper introduces a first-order algorithm that jointly learns a shared representation and task-specific parameters, with guaranteed efficiency. Notably, it converges in $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1)$ iterations and attains a \emph{near-optimal} estimation error of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(dk/(TN))$, \emph{improving} over existing likelihood-based methods by a factor of $k$, where $d$, $k$, $T$, $N$ denote input dimension, representation dimension, task count, and samples per task, respectively. Our results justify that likelihood-based first-order methods can efficiently solve the MTL problem.
